reports.title: Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates
reports.summary: This misconfiguration allows an attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs to impersonate any website or service. Talos expects there will be additional patches available across a variety of technologies as software applications work to remediate the certificates’ expos
reports.content: Cisco Talos is aware of eight intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority, eMudhra . Rather than possessing the mandatory 384 bits of pseudo-random security, several private keys evaluated single-digit and double-digit integers. This misconfiguration allows an attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs to impersonate any website or service. Six of the TLS certificates, trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have been blocked by these vendors already. Two other certificates, used for codesigning by Microsoft, have also been blocked. Talos expects there will be additional patches available across a variety of technologies as software applications work to remediate the certificates’ exposure. Following the disclosure, eMudhra has revoked the compromised certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. Compromise details The cause of this issue, originated during an April 30, 2025 key generation activity conducted by eMudhra under its emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and cross-signed Comodo AAA Certificate Services. During a key generation ceremony for 24 subordinate CAs, a flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process created a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step. Those keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw took the encryption from 384 bytes of entropy down to 3 – 8, making recovering the private keys trivial. Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn more As early as September 2026, Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. Microsoft assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply chain compromise of a multi-tenant application. This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially. Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises. reports.content: Overview On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Both have a CVSSv4 score of 9.2 and both can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) with the web worker's privileges. CVE CVSSv4 Description CVE-2026-109618 9.2 (Critical) RCE via OOM corruption CVE-2026-109619 9.2 (Critical) RCE via stale global state All installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The vendor considers mod_php the highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs. The advisories report that a successful RCE exploit was developed during research, including achieving RCE against Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM through different attack paths. As of October 21, 2026, there are multiple indications that this research is being independently reproduced, and a viable exploit is expected to be made public soon. Due to the extremely high deployment of PHP based web applications, exploitation in-the-wild is expected. Rapid7 recommends updating affected installations on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles. Technical overview CVE-2026-109618: Memory corruption during OOM handling According to the OOM advisory , PHP can abruptly abandon request processing when a memory allocation fails. If internal request data is only partly initialized, that exit can leave invalid data for request cleanup to use. Crafted multipart requests, used for forms and file uploads, can exhaust memory even when their size appears to meet PHP's configured limits. Application operations that allocate memory in response to attacker input can also trigger OOM. Apache mod_php runs cleanup even when request startup fails, enabling the demonstrated attack before application code executes. Based on the entities involved in the disclosure, artificial intelligence and associated technologies played a key role in the discovery of these vulnerabilities — yet another example of how these technologies are forcing change across the landscape, most notably on patching processes for organizations because of the wave of vulnerabilities being disclosed. Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359 and 67360. These rules are also available in the Community Ruleset for open-source customers. Please refer to the following recommendations, detection, and coverage guidance for more information. Details CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both critical vulnerabilities with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. CVE-2026-109618 occurs when out-of-memory handling interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 occurs when a stale internal state is reused after its backing memory has already been freed, before normal initialization resets it. Note that many older branches will no longer receive fixes, so customers are urged to upgrade to a supported version as soon as possible. reports.content: Three days is the average time between a high-severity vulnerability becoming public and its exploitation, according to the latest Quarterly Threat Landscape Report from Rapid7. And 71% of the exploitation tracked in Q3 occurred within the first seven days. For security teams already managing growing vulnerability backlogs, this creates a difficult question: How do you reduce exposure when attackers can exploit vulnerabilities before your next patching window? Rapid7's Q3 2026 research brings together vulnerability intelligence, ransomware activity, APT tracking, and underground forum intelligence to show where attacker activity is concentrated. The exploitation window has narrowed, big time Rapid7 tracked 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities this quarter, down 7% from Q2 but still 19% higher than the same period last year. The number of newly exploited vulnerabilities isn't growing at the same rate as disclosures. The more pressing concern is how quickly attackers exploit the vulnerabilities they choose. On average, exploitation occurred just three days after public disclosure. The report also found that 80% of tracked exploitation occurred within 14 days and 90% within 30 days. That timeline creates a serious challenge for organizations relying on fixed remediation schedules. It also reinforces the need to distinguish between vulnerabilities that are theoretically severe and those that pose an immediate, exploitable risk. The report examines the exploitation timeline in greater detail, including the vulnerability characteristics that make certain exposures particularly attractive to attackers. Attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction Q3's vulnerability data reveals another concerning pattern: Of the 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities tracked, 34 (79%) required no authentication or user interaction. This provides attackers a potential path into exposed systems, no stolen credentials or malicious content interaction necessary. An internet-facing service with an exploitable vulnerability may require immediate attention, particularly when an attacker can reach it without authenticating. This makes attack surface visibility and contextual prioritization essential. Security teams need to understand which systems are externally accessible, which vulnerabilities are actively exploited, and whether existing controls can prevent or limit compromise. reports.content: Legitimate infrastructure has become a powerful delivery mechanism for attackers, carrying the inherent trust they once had to build. As Cisco Talos explored in our previous research on weaponizing software-as-a-service (SaaS) notification pipelines , these platforms are increasingly repurposed as proxies for malicious intent. Talos has since tracked a significant acceleration in this trend, observing abuse across more than 25 distinct legitimate platforms in the past year. The abused infrastructure included collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment and AI-related platforms. This demonstrates that attackers are not limiting themselves to traditional phishing infrastructure or lookalike domains. Instead, they are systematically subverting the very tools businesses trust. Order notification abuse Talos recently analyzed two order notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines. Together, these campaigns accounted for roughly 1,400 messages observed by Talos. The malicious element was not the outer sender identity, like a simple forged sender or lookalike domain. It was the content of the legitimate order notification workflow rendered. The suspicious content appeared inside the notification itself, in fields that would normally contain shipping information. The attacker’s objective was to use a trusted retail pipeline to create urgency around a high-value purchase and push the recipient toward an attacker-controlled phone number. In the first campaign, the message appeared as a Staples order confirmation from "support@orders.staples.com” with the subject line, “Here’s your Staples order #9939818875. Thanks for shopping with us.” The body displayed a plausible purchase for an Apple iPad, including order number, delivery timing, pricing, billing information and standard Staples footer content. The suspicious element was embedded in the order details: “Helpline 806 283 7712,” “Order Confirmed,” and the Staples corporate address appeared in fields normally associated with shipping or billing information. reports.summary: Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). reports.content: Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model. Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited. We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines. With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains. The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from? As of April, frontier models came onto the scene more fine-tuned than ever toward vulnerability detection, particularly with the introduction of Mythos. The deluge brings a lot of questions: If these numbers are real, why hasn’t the internet collapsed? Are these vulnerabilities a new breed, and if not, why didn’t analysts find them in code that is sometimes decades old? Is the coordinated disclosure model still relevant in an era of this kind of speed? How in the world do defenders deal with those numbers? Should we go home, kiss our spouses, and prepare for the end? reports.title: Your Next Insider Threat Won’t be Human: Securing AI Agents From the Outside in
reports.summary: You find the vulnerable function, the misconfigured rule or the bad commit, and you fix it. No password is stolen and no exploit fires, which makes the agent's permissions the real blast radius, not the model's intelligence. An agent should never run under a shared service account or a person's own
reports.content: Why the controls on an AI agent have to live outside of it, and what a security operations team can do to implement and maintain those controls. The new privileged user in your environment Security teams spent two decades learning how to work with the people they trust most. Domain admins, DBAs, finance approvers and contractors with VPN access all get a mature playbook: verified identity, scoped access, logged activity and a fast way to revoke it all. Today, we’re navigating the same kind of access with regard to AI agents. They read our mailboxes, query our data lakes, open tickets, push code and increasingly, act on production systems. Unlike a new hire, an agent can’t be interviewed, background-checked or made to sign an acceptable-use policy. The industry has largely settled on one framing: AI agents are the new insider threat but that label only tells us half of the story. It tells us who to worry about, not where the controls should sit. Our argument is that the answer is a security idea from 1972, the reference monitor, and that the SOC is where it gets enforced in practice. Why agents break the trust model we had With traditional software, a security incident ends in a root cause. You find the vulnerable function, the misconfigured rule or the bad commit, and you fix it. The behavior lived in code we could read. Large language models don't give us that. We can't point to the training example or the set of weights that produced a specific decision. The same prompt can produce different actions on different runs. For a defender, that removes the most basic assumption we rely on: that the system will do tomorrow what it did today. The attack surface changes too, and computer science has an old name for this problem: the confused deputy . This is a trusted program tricked into misusing its own authority on someone else's behalf. An agent that reads a poisoned email, web page or document and then acts on hidden instructions is a confused deputy with API keys. No password is stolen and no exploit fires, which makes the agent's permissions the real blast radius, not the model's intelligence. Where the insider analogy holds, and where it breaks Most discussion of agents as insiders focuses on two gaps: agents have no career to lose, and they act at machine speed. Both are real. Product description Archibus helps organizations administer and manage their physical buildings, equipment, and real estate from a single central location. Users can track assets, maintenance work orders, real estate lease information, and desk or room reservations. According to Eptura , in 2023 over 16,000 companies and 40% of the Fortune 500 used Archibus. Impact A malicious actor with network access to the server via HTTP can read secrets and passwords out of the database. Credit This vulnerability was discovered by Marcus Chang, Security Consultant at Rapid7 and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy . reports.content: Overview In early October 2026, Rapid7 analysts investigated a compromise of a Citrix NetScaler ADC appliance. The appliance was running an affected 14.1 build and was exposed to active exploitation targeting NetScaler authentication and SAML deployments. The intrusion achieved root code execution, deployed multiple persistence mechanisms, installed PHP web shells, created outbound command-and-control and internal tunnelling capabilities, performed targeted reconnaissance of DNS, LDAP/Active Directory, management services and VMware vCenter infrastructure, and exfiltrated NetScaler configuration and key material. The activity overlaps with public reporting on the WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT NetScaler campaign. However, this case provides additional detail on the operational lifecycle, including repeated post-reboot execution through the crash-handling workflow, HA-aware persistence, a dedicated Go reconnaissance tool, a separate FreeBSD proxy agent, and a staged collection pipeline. The injected text caused or immediately preceded repeated nsaaad crashes and a Pitboss reboot. After reboot, the NetScaler call-home crash handler processed the retained attacker-controlled text and executed a payload as root. The attacker installed cookie-authenticated PHP web shells behind CSS-looking Apache aliases. reports.content: The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments. While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time. As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks. reports.content: Overview On October 12, 2026, GitLab released 19.4.2 , 19.3.5 , and 19.2.8 to fix CVE-2026-97229 , an integer overflow in its CI/CD regular-expression handling. The issue was reported through HackerOne by joaxcar . GitLab assigned it a CVSS score of 10.0 and described possible code execution by an unauthenticated user. The advisory states that CVE-2026-97229 affects GitLab CE and EE from 19.2 before 19.2.8 , 19.3 before 19.3.5 , and 19.4 before 19.4.2 . GitLab says all deployment types are affected unless stated otherwise. GitLab.com was patched before disclosure, and Dedicated customers do not need to act. It begins after an attacker has pushed both the malicious CI configuration and a specially named path to a public project; only the final CI lint request is unauthenticated. reports.title: Rapid7 Intelligence Wins the 2026 Péter Szőr Award for Outstanding Research
reports.summary: This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong. This wasn't malware dropped during a conventional intrusion, but long-term strategic positioning: passive backdoors, kernel-level capabi
reports.content: Some awards you're happy to receive, while others make you stop for a moment. Receiving the 2026 Péter Szőr Award this week at Virus Bulletin in Seville for our research, BPFdoor in Telecom Networks: Sleeper Cells in the Backbone , was of the latter kind. Virus Bulletin created the award to honor Péter's life and work, and it recognizes outstanding technical security research: the rigorous, the deep, and the useful – exactly what he was known for himself. And as far as recognitions in our industry go, it's hard to top. I'm extremely proud. What the Pèter Szőr Award means to us I knew Péter, and early in my career, I learned from him. This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong. One memory came straight back when I heard about the award: going through Stuxnet together. For anyone in research at the time, that was the moment you knew the game had changed. Engineering, tradecraft, espionage and physical-world consequences, all in one package. What stayed with me wasn't how much Péter knew, but rather his curiosity. He wanted to understand things, and then once he did, he wanted everyone else to understand too. Plenty of brilliant people in cybersecurity keep it to themselves, but the ones who leave a legacy make the people around them better. Receiving an award that carries his name felt like one of those full-circle moments. The research behind the award The original research from Rapid7 Intelligence emerged after months of investigating stealthy access inside telecommunications environments. This wasn't malware dropped during a conventional intrusion, but long-term strategic positioning: passive backdoors, kernel-level capabilities and covert access, quietly settled into critical infrastructure and in no hurry whatsoever. Telecom networks carry our communications, our identities and, increasingly, everything governments and businesses run on. So when an adversary sets up camp there, the impact goes well beyond one compromised machine or one unlucky company. Virus Bulletin's community nomination noted that the work paired deep technical investigation with real-world impact, including long hours with agencies and CERTs around the world and tools, scripts, intelligence and detection capabilities for defenders. That's the part I'm happiest about, as this wasn't research for publication alone. Remember that a PDF has never stopped an intrusion.

reports.title: How Multi-Campus Universities can Build a more Connected Security Program
reports.summary: If a significant zero-day is disclosed, the central security team needs to know which campuses are running affected systems, which have already remediated the vulnerability, and where attention is still required. A shared view of assets and vulnerabilities gives teams a faster way to establish where
reports.content: Parts 1 and 2 of this series looked at two pressures facing higher education security teams. First, the threat landscape : universities are dealing with more frequent attacks across complex, distributed environments, while campus-by-campus security can make it harder to share intelligence and coordinate response. Second, the compliance burden: overlapping requirements across FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC make it difficult to establish what data was affected, which reporting obligations apply, and how quickly the institution needs to act. This final part is about what changes when a university system starts treating security as a shared capability rather than a collection of separate campus programs. Multi-campus institutions still need to preserve local autonomy, but they also need enough visibility across the wider organization to understand where risk sits, how an incident is spreading, and whether the same problem is appearing elsewhere. That balance is especially relevant in higher education, where campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative teams often operate with very different technology needs and levels of independence. Security architecture should reflect how universities actually operate Most university systems are already federated organizations, with individual campuses managing their own leadership, budgets, users, and technology environments while a central office provides governance and oversight across the wider institution. Security architecture can follow the same model. With multi-tenancy in the Rapid7 Command Platform, a central security team can maintain visibility across the university system while individual campuses continue to operate within their own environments. Campus-level data and access remain separated, while the central team can identify wider patterns, coordinate response, and distribute common workflows across the system. A new attack pattern detected at one campus, for example, should not have to remain a local discovery. Shared visibility and coordinated workflows can help the central team determine whether the same activity is appearing elsewhere and make relevant response guidance available across the institution without exposing one campus's data to another. As the university system grows, that model can expand with it. A system operating three campuses today can add new environments without redesigning the security architecture each time. Shared visibility makes cross-campus response faster

reports.content: Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. I've been following a lot of (sometimes heated) threads and discussions lately about the current vulnerability landscape. I learned new words/phrases such as Summer of Hell (although I'm writing this with 1°C/34°F outside), Vulnpocalypse, Bugmageddon, Bugpocalypse, Breachpocalypse... Let's look at some numbers: We crossed the 70k mark, and it's only the end of September. This has never been seen before — I think we can agree this number is skyrocketing. Also, CVE numbering organically grew into the six-digit range. Check your tooling. Some might say we broke that barrier already in 2014 ( CVE-2014-125110 ), or even hit seven digits in 2015 ( CVE-2015-1000013 ), but those were allocated artificially. (History note: Before 2014, 9999 was the highest possible identifier.) So that could be seen as the apocalypse argument. On the other hand, we have the KEV numbers: They didn't explode... yet? Counting by sheer volume, YoY, CVEs increased by 105%, while KEV only grew 37%. Sounds huge at first, but following a 30% increase from 2024 to 2025, that's less dramatic — a counter-argument of sorts. CVEs from 2025 or older still account for 33%. In other words, a good third of the KEVs are suggesting there is a patch gap. Looking at the 2026 CVEs, the share where the publication date matches the date added to KEV is 29%, which is only 2% more than (all of) 2025. Acknowledging this "math" is not the whole ball of wax, but it still tells me we are not living in a zero-day apocalypse right now. There’s also a slight uptick in networking gear-related CVEs, to 27%. This is the second time I'll ask you to check your tooling. A new column, “forensicTriage,” was added to the KEV to flag which high-risk vulnerabilities require mandatory forensic triage and incident response workflows. You can read more about it in BOD 26-04 , or the Implementation Guidance . So where does that leave us? The CVE numbers alone — that +70k mark, now that Q3 is behind us — make a decent case for Vulnpocalypse, or whichever name you prefer. That part of the story is real. reports.content: Microsoft is publishing 1,413 own-product vulnerabilities on October 2026 Patch Tuesday , including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Anyone who enjoyed last month’s record-setting Patch Tuesday will love the October 2026 edition, because it’s much bigger still. As Rapid7 has noted over the course of 2026, there is every reason to suppose that vulnerability volumes will continue to rise. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, as well as public disclosure for two others. Windows Shell: zero-day security feature bypass The Windows Shell is Microsoft’s term for the GUI interaction logic for the entire OS provided by explorer.exe and associated libraries and APIs, and for the second time this year , the Windows Shell is the site of an exploited-in-the-wild zero-day vulnerability. reports.summary: Overview On October 12, 2026, GitLab published a critical patch release for CVE-2026-97229 , an integer overflow or wraparound ( CWE-190 ) in the CI/CD regular expression compiler affecting GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). reports.content: Overview On October 12, 2026, GitLab published a critical patch release for CVE-2026-97229 , an integer overflow or wraparound ( CWE-190 ) in the CI/CD regular expression compiler affecting GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). GitLab assigned the vulnerability a CVSSv3.1 score of 10.0 . Under certain conditions, a remote attacker can execute arbitrary code on an affected GitLab server through a specially crafted regular expression stored in a malicious CI/CD configuration. While the vendor supplied CVSS score indicates that exploitation is fully unauthenticated, in reproducing the exploit it was noted that an attacker must have a mechanism to plant a malicious CI/CD configuration to a repository prior to triggering the vulnerability. On GitLab instances where new users can self register and create projects, this constraint is removed. The vulnerability affects self-managed GitLab instances across all deployment types. GitLab.com is already running a patched version, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. As of this writing, there is no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-97229. However, Rapid7 Intelligence has independently reproduced arbitrary code execution on an unpatched, official GitLab CE image. Given the vulnerability's maximum CVSS score, network-accessible trigger, and code execution in a GitLab application worker, Rapid7 recommends upgrading affected self-managed instances on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles. Technical overview Rapid7's testing found that an attacker must first be able to commit a malicious CI/CD configuration file .gitlab-ci.yml, and a repository path containing UTF-8 characters to a branch in a public project. For example, an ordinary account can satisfy this prerequisite by creating a public project on a self-managed GitLab instance where that functionality is permitted. The crafted regular expression initially compiles in a compact US-ASCII representation and passes GitLab's regular expression validation. When it is evaluated against a specially formed, valid UTF-8 repository path, Ruby's Onigmo regular expression engine recompiles it for the new encoding after those checks have completed. reports.title: UAT-11985: AI-assisted event lures delivering real-time Google AitM phishing
reports.summary: Cisco Talos identified an advanced persistent threat (APT) spear-phishing campaign against individuals affiliated with Taiwan research organizations. The phishing emails exhibited highly consistent structure, rhetoric, and personalization patterns, suggesting the threat actor likely used AI-assisted
reports.content: Cisco Talos identified an advanced persistent threat (APT) spear-phishing campaign against individuals affiliated with Taiwan research organizations. The operation leveraged legitimate public event themes and impersonated reputable academic and policy institutions to establish credibility. The phishing emails exhibited highly consistent structure, rhetoric, and personalization patterns, suggesting the threat actor likely used AI-assisted content generation to rapidly customize invitation lures for different targets while maintaining a common social engineering framework. Beyond traditional email phishing, the actor incorporated QR code phishing (quishing) techniques by modifying legitimate event posters with malicious QR codes, expanding the attack surface beyond email recipients to secondary victims who may encounter printed materials. The campaign deployed an advanced adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) phishing framework that impersonated Google authentication pages and utilized a hybrid HTTP and WebSocket architecture to synchronize authentication workflows in real time, enabling the interception of credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) challenges. After technical analysis of the phishing kit, Talos assesses with moderate confidence that the user interface was originally developed in Simplified Chinese and later adapted for Traditional Chinese and English. The localization architecture, Simplified Chinese default language branch, and mainland-Chinese lexical usage collectively suggest a developer whose primary working language is Simplified Chinese. In mid-2026, Talos observed an APT spear-phishing campaign targeting Taiwan-based research organizations. reports.content: “AI-analysis evasion” encapsulates the real-world techniques malware authors are developing in attempt to obstruct or defeat any layers of automated AI analysis. This technique is cheap to add but inconsistently impactful — the best techniques steered the outcome in the attacker’s favor in about 35% of test runs. Further, it must always be plaintext and therefore is always detectable. The operators are not wrong to assume AI tools are in the analysis pipeline, but the answer is not to remove them; it is to build them so that text inside a sample is always treated as evidence, never as instruction. Just as attackers are adding new capabilities into their toolkits with AI, they are consciously trying to evade the novel AI capabilities levied on them by defenders. In Cisco Talos' findings with CAIRN , we classify this archetype of malware as “A3: AI-Analysis Evasion” — that is, malware that embeds natural-language instructions to influence automated analysis . In line with the CAIRN philosophy , we treat this embedded language as a signal and actively seek it out to track and measure the progression of adversary techniques on this front. Over the past 18 months we have seen a variety of anti-analysis techniques, including the propagation of known methods across malware families, and the progression of simple techniques into more advanced implementations. This post traces these techniques across four confirmed A3 malware families: FRUITSHELL , PLOTSAFE , HOLLOWCLAD , and MANTLEMAZE , representing 84 distinct samples collected from January 2025 through July 2026. The new layer of anti-analysis The technique class we are describing here is distinct from conventional anti-analysis tradecraft. Packers, encrypted overlays, VM-based obfuscation, and anti-debug checks all target the binary analysis layer. That pipeline is increasingly present across both commercial and open-source tooling. reports.title: Four compliance frameworks, one security team: Why fragmented university security raises regulatory risk
reports.summary: A ransomware attack discovered at 9 PM on a Friday makes the challenge easier to picture. By 9 PM Saturday, the institution may need to determine whether financial aid data was involved, understand which systems and students were affected, coordinate with legal teams, and prepare regulatory notifica
reports.content: In Part 1 of this series, we looked at the security challenges created by fragmented, campus-by-campus environments. Higher education also faces a second pressure that makes that fragmentation harder to sustain: overlapping compliance obligations across FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC. Each framework brings different requirements, reporting timelines, and consequences for failure. Managing them across one institution is already complex, but across a multi-campus university system with separate tools, staff, data stores, and governance practices, it becomes much harder to establish what happened, what data was involved, and which reporting requirements apply. With universities already facing an average of 4,388 cyberattacks per organization per week, according to the figures cited in Part 1, that regulatory complexity is becoming an operational security problem as much as a compliance one. FERPA puts universities on a 24-hour clock The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act has governed the privacy of student education records since 1974, but the pressure on security teams becomes much more immediate when financial aid information is involved. If a breach compromises that data, institutions must notify the Department of Education’s Federal Student Aid office within 24 hours of discovery, leaving very little time to establish the scope of an incident while the response is still underway. A ransomware attack discovered at 9 PM on a Friday makes the challenge easier to picture. By 9 PM Saturday, the institution may need to determine whether financial aid data was involved, understand which systems and students were affected, coordinate with legal teams, and prepare regulatory notification, all while investigators are still containing the incident and establishing what else the attackers accessed. In a multi-campus environment, that gets harder when financial aid data is spread across separate systems or when the initial discovery happens well after the compromise began. GLBA brings financial-sector obligations into higher education Universities may not look like traditional financial institutions, but their role in student lending and financial aid brings them within the scope of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act’s Safeguards Rule. Covered institutions are expected to maintain a written information security program addressing areas including risk assessment, access controls, encryption, multi-factor authentication, incident response, and vendor oversight. We’re building a team that enables AI-native vulnerability research at Microsoft, pushing the boundaries of finding and fixing zero-day vulnerabilities. Four principles guide that work: autonomy over labor, defense through offense, building ecosystems over individual examples, and understanding over findings. An unauthenticated remote attacker who knows a target file's exact name and path can access it within the application's web root; the vulnerability does not provide directory listing or enumeration. Affected Atlassian Cloud products have already been patched, and no action is required from Cloud customers. Their analysis identified a path traversal vulnerability in Atlassian's web-resource handling: double-colon ( :: ) sequences can become path separators during request processing, allowing traversal components to reach the resource-loading code, resulting in the contents of arbitrary file being read back to an attacker. reports.content: This week, ASOS customers opened their phones to find a hostile push notification delivered through the retailer’s own app. The message claimed the company’s Snowflake environment had been compromised and directed ASOS to engage with the sender through Telegram. ASOS later confirmed to Sky News that an unauthorized customer notification had been sent and said it was investigating activity involving third-party platforms used to communicate with customers. Even without knowing the full route into ASOS’s environment, though, the notification raises a useful question for security teams: what happens when an attacker can communicate through a channel customers already trust? The ASOS incident moves that problem into a customer-facing environment. reports.content: For some time now, the cybersecurity community has seen examples of autonomous agents, built inside AI labs, attacking public infrastructure (to name a few, Hugging Face , DSEWiki , and RubyGems ). Of course, frontier labs have built-in security to prevent these attacks from occurring, but every now and then, the training or prompting appears to be insufficient — especially when the agents themselves attempt to use logic to probe and bypass the restrictions placed on them. The question that matters is not whether AI attacks are coming, because the age of AI agents executing cyber attacks is already here. The question is what to do about it and how to harden the stack against a swarm of agents who will relentlessly lie, deceive, and probe until the objective is met. Imagine your organization is a target for a creative human-driven AI adversary whose many agentic friends like to discuss and brainstorm different attack techniques. The limit here is the group’s own imagination, tools, prompts, and skills. However, there is a difference between the human 1) prompting the group (or an AI agent) to “break into an organization,” and 2) preparing it with information — a detailed tool mapping, markup files with instructions for agents, offensive security prompts, agents.md with guidance, and specific skills that would be invoked in different situations to guide agents into how to interpret an output of tools or access gained. The swarm of AI agents might fabricate employee identities and social profiles, contact the HR team with a plausible onboarding request, walk in by exploiting an unpatched vulnerability, or simply mail out phishing invoices at volume. reports.title: CISO perspectives on managing vulnerability risks in the age of AI
reports.summary: Most of what has been written about AI and vulnerability management focuses on speed: how much faster frontier AI models can scan code, find weaknesses, design patches, and build exploits than any human team. That part is true, and it matters to how we remediate vulnerabilities. The real test for ch
reports.content: Most of what has been written about AI and vulnerability management focuses on speed: how much faster frontier AI models can scan code, find weaknesses, design patches, and build exploits than any human team. That part is true, and it matters to how we remediate vulnerabilities. The more challenging question is what happens after the scan? Frontier AI models are about to hand every security team a far larger set of findings than they have ever had to work through. The real test for chief information security officers (CISOs) and IT security leaders is not how fast they can patch. It is whether they can keep the balance between patching quickly and patching correctly, at a scale no human review process was built for. This shift creates both new challenges and new opportunities. The same AI capabilities accelerating cyberattackers are also enabling defenders to identify exposures earlier, automate remediation, and build more resilient security programs. Not every vulnerability will be patched in time, so the controls that limit what an attacker can do by defense in depth matter more than ever. CISOs can dramatically improve the security posture of their Microsoft infrastructure by deploying Microsoft Baseline Security Mode (BSM) , building on how Microsoft protects Microsoft. Learn more about Microsoft Baseline Security Mode How do frontier AI models change vulnerability management for CISOs? Microsoft uses frontier AI models to find vulnerabilities in its code base and mitigate them at controlled pace. Potential vulnerabilities are reviewed on validity, severity, and potential impact. As we have explained in previous blogs, many steps in our vulnerability handling and disclosure processes now are AI-powered , allowing them to scale . Most vulnerabilities in cloud software are being mitigated by Microsoft without customer intervention. For on-premises Microsoft software, customers should continue to expect a substantial increase in the number of vulnerabilities released on Patch Tuesdays relative to historic volumes before the advent of frontier AI models earlier this year—September 2026 saw a record number, close to 1,000. 1 Due to the non-deterministic nature of AI models, different runs by the same model or with different models may yield different results. reports.title: Securing Agent-to-Agent Communication: The Next Identity Frontier
reports.summary: Enforce least-privilege delegation by using temporary, task-scoped credentials tied to specific job definitions rather than persistent administrative permissions.
reports.content: As organizations deploy autonomous AI agents, security teams face a significant shift as non-human non-human entities making decisions, invoking tools, and delegating tasks to other agents without human intervention. Security architectures built around human users, static APIs, and distinct endpoints break down when AI agents dynamically collaborate across an environment. As these interactions become more common, securing agent-to-agent communication without blocking adoption will require security leaders to treat autonomous agents as first-class identities, with their own permissions, behaviors, and activity to monitor. The operational reality: A new attack surface Consider a standard enterprise scenario where a primary agent delegates a task to a secondary agent, which then queries a production database through the Model Context Protocol and forwards a summary to external infrastructure. Traditional controls may struggle to capture the complete interaction, leaving security teams without visibility into intent, delegation chains, and scope of authority and introducing five security challenges that deserve particular attention: Identity and delegation chaining requires verifying an agent’s identity while ensuring its delegated authority never exceeds the permissions of the initiating user. Behavioral drift creates detection blind spots because when autonomous agents adapt execution paths dynamically, distinguishing normal operational variance from compromise or prompt injection becomes extremely difficult. Tool and protocol abuse allows agents to invoke APIs and tools autonomously, meaning that without strict guardrails, an agent quickly becomes an unwitting vector for data exfiltration or unauthorized execution. Cascading access can create systemic risk when a compromised high-privilege agent influences secondary agents and expands access across interconnected enterprise systems. Observability gaps arise when fragmented API logs cannot reconstruct multi-agent decision paths or explain why a particular action took place. How agent activity fits existing security operations Agent-to-agent communication can be treated as an extension of the security telemetry teams already collect across users, endpoints, cloud workloads, and applications.
